statement: Ana can paint a fence on her own in 6 hours. When Ana and Ben paint it together, each at their usual speed, it takes 4 hours. How many hours would Ben take to paint the fence on his own?

choices.misconception: I subtracted the times, 6 - 4, as if Ben's time were the difference.
I found that Ben paints one third of the fence in the 4 hours together, and wrote 3 from the fraction instead of a number of hours.
I assumed Ana and Ben work at the same speed, so each alone would take twice the 4 hours, but Ana alone takes only 6.
I added the two times, 6 + 4, as if working together made the job take longer.

hints: How much of the fence is painted in one hour?
Think of the fence as made of equal parts. Find the fraction of the fence painted per hour together and by Ana alone; the difference is Ben's share per hour.
Together they paint $\frac{1}{4}$ of the fence each hour, and Ana paints $\frac{1}{6}$.

solutions.reliable: Together they paint $\frac{1}{4}$ of the fence per hour, and Ana paints $\frac{1}{6}$ per hour. So Ben paints $\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{6} = \frac{3}{12} - \frac{2}{12} = \frac{1}{12}$ of the fence per hour, and on his own he needs 12 hours. The transferable idea: in work problems, add or subtract rates (parts per hour), never times.
solutions.elegant: Split the fence into 12 equal strips. Ana paints 2 strips an hour, and together they paint 3 strips an hour, so Ben paints 1 strip an hour and needs 12 hours. Choosing a total that both times divide turns the fractions into whole numbers.

whyOnTest: Work-rate questions test that rates add while times do not; working back from a joint time means subtracting rates.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
